title: Weak Supervision for Traders: Combining Several Noisy Labeling Heuristics into One Probabilistic Label (Snorkel-Style)
text:
Introduction
Every rule-based signal you have ever written is a noisy vote, not a ground truth. An RSI crossback, a moving-average cross, a MACD flip—each one fires on a real pattern, but each one is also wrong a meaningful fraction of the time, and none of them agree with each other as often as you would like. The usual fix is to pick your favorite one, or to AND a couple of them together and call it a filter. Both approaches throw away information: a favorite signal ignores the others entirely, and an AND-gate treats every input as equally trustworthy, which none of them are - and it also throws away every bar where the favorite signal abstains but two others agree strongly.
This article builds something different: a small generative model in the style of Stanford's Snorkel. It takes five independent, cheap, noisy technical heuristics (none accurate enough to trade alone) and learns how much to trust each one purely from their agreement patterns on live bars. No labeled training set, no manually assigned confidence weights, no grid search over LF weights. Expectation-Maximization does the weighting dynamically as market conditions change, and it does it from the same kind of evidence a human discretionary trader uses when deciding which of their indicators to believe this week: not "was this indicator right," which nobody can know in real time, but "does this indicator keep siding with what the others are converging on."
I built this as an MQL5 Expert Advisor with an EM fitting engine in a shared include library. I wired it to five MetaTrader indicator-backed heuristics and ran it across six Strategy Tester configurations (three symbols × two timeframes), alongside an unweighted majority-vote baseline. The results are reported exactly as produced by the terminal. This includes the one configuration where EM's per-LF weighting did not help, and the fact that none of the twelve runs turned a profit. The interesting finding in this article isn't "this system makes money" - it doesn't, as shipped. It's that a model with zero access to trade outcomes can still estimate, from vote agreement alone, which of five noisy heuristics deserves more say in the fused decision, and that trusting it over an unweighted vote changes the resulting P&L - on this test matrix mostly by losing a little less, though the statistical check in the results section shows that difference is too small to separate from noise.
This is a labeling and signal-fusion technique, not a strategy with an edge baked in. The five labeling functions here are illustrative - RSI, an EMA cross, Bollinger reversion, a MACD flip, and a candle proxy - chosen because they are common, cheap, and genuinely uncorrelated enough to make the fusion problem real. Swap in your own heuristics; the EM engine and the trust-weighting idea are what this article is actually about.
The idea in one picture
Each of the five labeling functions (LFs) looks at the closed bar and returns one of three things: a buy vote, a sell vote, or an abstain, when it has no opinion. Those five votes go into
CWeakLabelModel
, which has learned - purely from historical agreement patterns - how accurate each LF tends to be, and folds that into a single fused probability of the next move being a buy.
Fig. 1. Signal-fusion pipeline: five labeling functions vote, the EM label model weighs them by learned reliability, and the result is a single P(Buy).
The model that does the fusing has two kinds of parameters: alpha_j , one per labeling function, the model's own estimate - under the latent-variable assumptions, with no ground truth to check it against - of how often LF
j
's vote agrees with the inferred (not observed) label when it doesn't abstain, and a single class prior pi , the model's running estimate of how often "buy" is the right call in the current regime. Both are found with Expectation-Maximization, run purely on the LF vote history - never on price outcomes, never on a hand-labeled dataset. This is the core trick borrowed from Snorkel's data-programming line of work: you can recover a useful estimate of each labeling source's reliability from nothing but a matrix of votes, provided the sources are not all wrong in the same correlated way at once.
E-step: q_i = P(Y=+1 | votes_i) via log-sum-exp over
log(pi) + sum_j log(alpha_j) or log(1 - alpha_j), by vote agreement
M-step: pi = mean(q_i) over the buffered window
alpha_j = weighted_correct_j / weighted_total_j, weighted by q_i
That is the entire mechanism, and it is genuinely that short - the whole EM loop is under forty lines of MQL5, shown in full in Section 4. An LF whose votes consistently land on the side the posterior favors gets a high alpha_j and more say in future fusions; an LF that is basically coin-flipping against the consensus gets clamped down toward the floor. There's no separate training phase - the model refits on a rolling window every InpRefitEveryBars bars, so its opinion of each LF drifts as market conditions change, without you ever telling it what "changed." Section 10 shows exactly what got learned across six real markets, and it is not the same ranking twice.
The five labeling functions
CLabelingFunctions
owns five native MetaTrader indicator handles and exposes one Vote* method per heuristic, plus a wrapper that collects all five votes for one bar in a single call. Every method reads the CLOSED bar at the given shift and never repaints - shift 0 is never touched from
OnTick
, and every buffer read is guarded with a
CopyBuffer()
length check that returns an abstain rather than a garbage value if history isn't ready yet.

60

The abstain value matters more than it looks - it's what lets the model treat "this LF had nothing to say on this bar" differently from "this LF said sell." A naive scheme that forces every LF to vote on every bar would corrupt the EM fit, because a forced vote on a bar the LF genuinely can't read is noise dressed up as evidence. Keeping abstain as a real third state is what makes the vote-agreement statistics actually mean something.

LF1 fires on an RSI crossback through the classic 30/70 extremes - not on the extreme touch itself, but on the reversal back through it, which is the part that actually correlates with a turn. Touching 28 and staying there is not a signal here; crossing back above 30 after having been below it is:
CLabelingFunctions::VoteRsiExtreme

LF2 is a short-lookback fast/slow EMA cross, deliberately built from different periods than the EA's own longer trend filter (Section 6) so the two never just repeat the same signal under different names - if they used the same lookback, EM would effectively be double-counting one underlying feature and inflating its apparent reliability:

LF3 votes on a Bollinger Band touch-and-reversion: the prior bar has to actually pierce the band, and this bar has to close back inside it. A bar that merely brushes the band without piercing it, or pierces it and keeps going, gets no vote - this is a reversion signal, and it should only fire on an actual reversion, not on volatility expansion in the same direction:
CLabelingFunctions::VoteBollingerReversion

LF4 is the simplest of the five - a MACD histogram sign flip, main minus signal crossing zero. It's included specifically because it's a momentum signal rather than a reversion one, which gives the ensemble a genuinely different failure mode than LF1 and LF3, both of which are mean-reversion in spirit:

LF5 is a candle-pattern proxy that catches both an engulfing bar and a pin-bar off the same body-to-range ratio, rather than shipping two separate LFs for what is really one idea - a small body dominated by one wick, or a full reversal of the prior bar's body. The 30% body-fraction cutoff for the pin-bar case and the 2x wick-to-body ratio were picked to keep this LF selective rather than chatty; a looser threshold fires on almost every bar and stops being informative:

The generative label model
CWeakLabelModel
is the part doing the actual weak-supervision work. It keeps a fixed-capacity ring buffer of past vote rows, a learned accuracy per LF, and a learned class prior, and exposes
Fit()
to re-run EM and
Predict()
to fuse a fresh vote row once fitted.
SLFStats - per-labeling-function learned statistics

};

The core of the fusion is
PosteriorBuy()
: given one vote row and the current alpha/prior estimates, it computes the log-posterior for buy and sell under a naive-Bayes-style independence assumption across LFs, then normalizes back to a probability. Working in log-space here isn't a style choice - multiplying five or more probability terms directly underflows to zero in double precision faster than you'd expect, especially once alpha_j is close to its 0.999 ceiling and several LFs agree strongly. Summing logs and only exponentiating once, at the very end, via a log-sum-exp with the max subtracted out first, keeps every intermediate value in a numerically sane range:

That is the actual mixture-density log-likelihood, not a stand-in built from the already-normalized posterior, so the standard EM monotonicity guarantee genuinely applies: each E-step/M-step pair cannot decrease it, and watching it stop moving is a mathematically sound stopping rule, not a heuristic guess at "probably converged by now":

Notice what
Fit()
never touches: price, P&L, or any outcome label. It only ever looks at how the five vote columns agree and disagree with each other across the buffered window. An LF that regularly sides with the emerging consensus earns a high alpha_j . One that is essentially noise is clamped toward WS_ALPHA_FLOOR (0.501). The floor assumes adversarial LFs are rare and prevents
MathLog()
domain errors near zero. In real runs on the rolling windows used in this article, convergence typically lands well inside the 50-iteration cap - the log-likelihood tends to stop moving meaningfully within 10-15 passes once the window has enough non-abstain votes to work with, which is worth knowing if you're tuning InpRollingWindowBars for a tighter refit cadence on your own instrument.
Once fitted, fusing a fresh vote row is a single call - this is the only method the EA calls on every single tick after warm-up, and it's deliberately cheap: no loop over the buffer, just five log-additions and one log-sum-exp:

(!m_is_fitted)

Majority vote: the baseline this article measures EM against
A weighted model is only interesting if it beats the thing it replaces. The honest baseline here isn't "no filter" - that wouldn't isolate what EM is actually contributing. It's the same five LFs combined the naive way, an unweighted majority vote where a reliable LF and a coin-flipping one carry identical influence:

This function counts buy votes and sell votes among the non-abstaining LFs and returns the buy share directly as a probability - no accuracy weighting, no prior, no log-space anything. It's about as close to "the simplest thing that could plausibly work" as a fusion rule gets, which is exactly what makes it a fair yardstick: any margin EM shows over this baseline is coming from the learned weighting, not from some other confound.

Risk management and order execution
None of the weak-supervision logic above matters if the EA can size a position wrong. Three helper functions in the same library carry a few non-negotiable risk rules for any order-sending EA - real margin checks via the terminal's own margin calculator rather than a hand-rolled approximation, a real minimum-stop-distance floor that accounts for a broker reporting zero on stops/freeze level, and clamping against both a broker's volume limit and its volume max, not just one of the two, since clamping to max alone can still leave a lot size above a broker's separate volume-limit cap on some symbols.
WsCalcSafeLot - margin- and broker-limit-clamped lot sizing

//| Compute a margin- and broker-limit-clamped lot size              |
//| Returns 0.0 if the risk-based lot cannot be honored at all       |
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
double
WsCalcSafeLot
(
const
string
symbol,
const
double
risk_money,
const
double
sl_distance_price,
const
ENUM_ORDER_TYPE
order_type)
  {
if
(sl_distance_price <=
0.0
)
return
(
0.0
);
double
tick_value =
SymbolInfoDouble
(symbol,SYMBOL_TRADE_TICK_VALUE);
double
tick_size  =
SymbolInfoDouble
(symbol,SYMBOL_TRADE_TICK_SIZE);
double
vol_step   =
SymbolInfoDouble
(symbol,SYMBOL_VOLUME_STEP);
double
vol_min    =
SymbolInfoDouble
(symbol,SYMBOL_VOLUME_MIN);
double
vol_max     =
SymbolInfoDouble
(symbol,SYMBOL_VOLUME_MAX);
double
vol_limit   =
SymbolInfoDouble
(symbol,SYMBOL_VOLUME_LIMIT);
if
(tick_value <=
0.0
|| tick_size <=
0.0
|| vol_step <=
0.0
)
return
(
0.0
);
//--- level 2: risk-formula lot, before any clamping
double
loss_per_lot = (sl_distance_price / tick_size) * tick_value;
if
(loss_per_lot <=
0.0
)
return
(
0.0
);
double
raw_lot = risk_money / loss_per_lot;
//--- level 2: normalize to the broker's volume step
double
lot =
MathFloor
(raw_lot / vol_step) * vol_step;
//--- level 2: rule (2) - below broker minimum means skip, never round up
if
(lot < vol_min)
return
(
0.0
);
//--- level 2: rule (4) - clamp to BOTH volume limit and volume max
if
(vol_max   >
0.0
) lot =
MathMin
(lot,vol_max);
if
(vol_limit >
0.0
) lot =
MathMin
(lot,vol_limit);

required_margin =
0.0
;
double

                  ?
SymbolInfoDouble
(symbol,SYMBOL_ASK)

SymbolInfoDouble
(symbol,SYMBOL_BID);

(
OrderCalcMargin
(order_type,symbol,lot,price,required_margin))
     {
double
free_margin =
AccountInfoDouble
(ACCOUNT_MARGIN_FREE);
while
(lot >
0.0
&& required_margin > free_margin)
        {
         lot -= vol_step;
         lot  =
MathFloor
(lot / vol_step) * vol_step;
if
(lot < vol_min)
           {
            lot =
0.0
;
break
;
           }
if
(!
OrderCalcMargin
(order_type,symbol,lot,price,required_margin))
           {

0.0
;
break
;

else
{

Print
(
"WsCalcSafeLot(",symbol,") OrderCalcMargin err="
,
GetLastError
());

(
0.0
);

(lot);

string

const

(symbol,SYMBOL_TRADE_STOPS_LEVEL);

SymbolInfoInteger
(symbol,SYMBOL_TRADE_FREEZE_LEVEL);

(symbol,SYMBOL_POINT);

((
double

double
)freeze_level_pts);

for: LF1 fires on an RSI crossback through the classic 30/70 extremes — not on the extreme touch itself, but on the reversal back through it, which is the part that actually correlates with a turn
LF2 is a short-lookback fast/slow EMA cross, deliberately built from different periods than the EA's own longer trend filter so the two never just repeat the same signal under different names
LF3 votes on a Bollinger Band touch-and-reversion: the prior bar has to actually pierce the band, and this bar has to close back inside it
LF4 is the simplest of the five — a MACD histogram sign flip, main minus signal crossing zero
LF5 is a candle-pattern proxy that catches both an engulfing bar and a pin-bar off the same body-to-range ratio, with a 30% body-fraction cutoff for the pin-bar case and a 2x wick-to-body ratio

non_fatal: Статья не содержит конкретного торгового правила входа — она описывает метод фьюзинга сигналов (слабого обучения), но не определяет, при каком значении P(Buy) или каком условии происходит вход. В тексте упоминается порог InpConfidenceThreshold = 0.65 и использование p_buy в OnTick(), но точное правило входа (например, 'если p_buy > 0.65 и тренд восходящий — открывать покупку') не приведено в виде завершённого, однозначного условия; оно распределено по коду и подразумевается, а не задано явно.

В статье отсутствует описание выхода из позиции и стоп-уровней как части сигнала — они вынесены в отдельный блок 'Trend Filter and Trade Management', но не интегрированы в логику слабого обучения; это допустимо, но делает правило неполным как автономное торговое правило.

Нет описания, как именно используется P(Buy) для принятия решения: например, не указано, сравнивается ли p_buy с порогом *и* проверяется ли направление тренда *одновременно*, и в какой логической комбинации (AND/OR). Хотя в коде есть g_model.IsFitted() и p_buy, полное условие входа не выделено как формула или чёткое правило в тексте.

judge.reject_reason: Статья не содержит конкретного торгового правила входа — она описывает метод фьюзинга сигналов (слабого обучения), но не определяет, при каком значении P(Buy) или каком условии происходит вход. В тексте упоминается порог InpConfidenceThreshold = 0.65 и использование p_buy в OnTick(), но точное правило входа (например, 'если p_buy > 0.65 и тренд восходящий — открывать покупку') не приведено в виде завершённого, однозначного условия; оно распределено по коду и подразумевается, а не задано явно. Отсутствует чёткое, детерминированное, полное условие входа с направлением и всеми необходимыми параметрами, записанное как единое правило. Это фатальный порок: невозможно составить из статьи полное детерминированное правило для проверки на закрытых барах спот-форекса.
judge.author_oos_metrics: Ни одна из двенадцати тестовых конфигураций (три символа × два таймфрейма) не показала прибыль; автор отмечает, что система не генерирует прибыль «как поставлена», а основной вывод — возможность оценки надёжности эвристик по их согласованности без доступа к результатам сделок.
judge.summary: Статья представляет метод слабого обучения (weak supervision) для фьюзинга пяти независимых технических эвристик (RSI crossback, EMA cross, Bollinger reversion, MACD histogram flip, candle proxy) с помощью EM-алгоритма, оценивающего их относительную надёжность по паттернам согласования голосов. Цель — не создание прибыльной стратегии, а построение вероятностной оценки P(Buy) без использования меток исходов сделок.
